At a deeper level, this grew out of an attempt to affirm human freedom of will against the idea that human action was already determined by a prior will.
This was the fundamental revolutionary drive of the Muʿtazilite movement from the beginning.

It is true that the Muʿtazila dealt with these questions through abstract and speculative reasoning. But that method was imposed on them by the conditions of their time: first, by the dominance of religious forms of knowledge, and second, by a period of transition from simple, direct thinking to more complex and indirect forms of thought.

None of this, however, could hide the basic character of Muʿtazilite thought. It stood in opposition to a faith-based view centered on the unseen, to the idea that faith should come before reason, and to the belief that absolute predestination controlled human action.

The leading Muʿtazilite thinkers belonged to the wider educated group that included jurists, scholars of hadith, and Qurʾanic commentators. At the same time, they were connected to the political camps and parties of their age.
Because of this, they had living ties with public opinion across the different classes of society, and their ideas and views found a response among the wider public.

What, then, should we say about the relationship between the Muʿtazila and the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn, under whom Muʿtazilism became the doctrine of the state and remained so under his brother al-Muʿtaṣim and then under al-Wāthiq ibn al-Muʿtaṣim?

We answered this question by arguing that, during his struggle with his brother al-Amīn for the caliphate, al-Maʾmūn supported urban social groups connected to the city economy: trade, money-changing and banking, handicraft production, and moneylending.
His brother al-Amīn, by contrast, was connected to the owners of agricultural estates among the princes, nobles, and major landholders.
Their struggle was therefore connected to the conflict between the rural economy and the urban economy.
Muʿtazilite ideas expressed the ambitions of the city’s different social groups to gain social and political positions that had previously been monopolized by landowning nobles.
Those nobles, in turn, adopted conservative thought as their ideology.
This interpretation of al-Maʾmūn’s position does not completely exclude his personal role. He was also a highly educated man with relatively open intellectual tendencies.
We based this conclusion on a historical theory about the economic conditions of that period, supported by sources and references that we regard as reliable.
The Ashʿarite stage of kalām began during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil in 232 AH/847 CE.

This was the period in which conservative forces hostile to the positive gains of al-Maʾmūn’s reign came to the fore. These forces gained control over the weak personality of al-Mutawakkil, whose main concern was luxury.
From this point began a campaign of persecution and repression against Muʿtazilite thought and against all the positive tendencies it contained.
What is striking, however, is that the Ashʿarite school could not completely eliminate the question of reason and its role. The historical process had already moved too far for that.
The Ashʿarites therefore raised the slogan of returning to the defence of the doctrine of the People of the Sunna through rational proofs. Ibn Khaldūn mentions this in the Muqaddima, p. 838.
But this slogan was little more than a formal accommodation to the results of historical development. The school still relied fundamentally on transmitted authority, not on reason.
In this chapter, we discussed several questions in which the Ashʿarites adopted the outward form of a rational method, and we showed in some detail why this rationalism remained formal.
It would have been wrong to study kalām without considering the place of the Imami Shiʿa within it.
In practice, they took part alongside the Muʿtazila and the Khārijites in discussing almost all the major questions of kalām.
Indeed, a large part of the principles and foundations of Shiʿi doctrine belongs directly to the field of kalām.
But Shiʿi doctrine also contains positions that differ sharply from one another and are sometimes even ideologically contradictory.

On one side, the doctrine is based on the Imamate. In Shiʿi theory, the Imamate is a divine right belonging to their Imams. This means denying the people the right to choose the caliph and, after the Prophet, making the Imam the central source of knowledge.

On the other side, the Shiʿa agree with the Muʿtazila on several basic questions connected to the rationalist method. These include resistance to an unjust ruler and the idea that reason itself can judge what is good and what is bad. They also come close to the Muʿtazilite position on human freedom of choice in one’s actions.
We therefore have two different positions. How are we to identify their real ideological place?
In our view, the more likely explanation is that their practical history forced them toward the positions they shared with the Muʿtazila.
They had repeatedly opposed both Umayyad and Abbasid rulers, and they had themselves suffered continuous and often tragic persecution.

These conditions pushed them toward those ideological positions even when they conflicted with the principle of the Imamate, which, in our view, represents the most extreme restriction on the role of reason.
At the same time, there were major thinkers among the Imami Shiʿa who made important contributions to kalām and philosophy, including Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, al-Balkhī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.

But the ideas they developed in these fields did not arise from the principles of the Shiʿi doctrine itself. They were independent intellectual efforts shaped by social and intellectual conditions that had no necessary connection to that doctrine.
For this reason, we do not think it is correct to attribute their ideas and positions simply to their identity as Shiʿis.
We then examined the relationship between kalām and philosophy.
This relationship existed from the very beginnings of Muʿtazilite thought.
Historical sources tell us that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, the founder of the Muʿtazilite school, read books of philosophy. The same was true of other major thinkers in the movement.
That is one kind of evidence.
Another comes from the nature of the questions they examined. These questions were philosophical by their very nature.

We can also see the connection in the way they thought about those questions and the methods they used. Their approach was the approach of philosophers and their method was philosophical, whether through their reliance on reason and the language of concepts or through their use of logical argument.
This clear relationship between kalām and philosophy made kalām a preparatory stage in the emergence of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

It was the stage in which Arab thought trained itself to think through concepts and categories. In other words, it learned the method of intellectual abstraction without which philosophical inquiry cannot take place.
But what were the limits of this relationship?
We tried to answer that question in two ways.
First, kalām and philosophy were each relatively independent stages in the development of Arab thought.
Second, we can define the boundary between them more clearly by looking at the function each one performed in its own historical period.
Kalām used philosophical thinking as a way of examining questions raised within Arab society after Islam, but it did so through religious inquiry into Islamic doctrine.

Philosophy, by contrast, appeared in Arab-Islamic society after kalām had reached maturity. It examined existence, nature, society, and thought as concepts in their own right. Through these concepts, the material world was reflected indirectly as a particular society with its own historical conditions, characteristics, and forms of social relations.
Philosophy therefore differed from kalām, first, because it began from concepts rather than from social questions raised directly in society.
Second, it did not take Islamic doctrine as the foundation of its inquiry.

It did try to hide the contradiction between the conclusions reached through philosophical investigation and the doctrines of Islam. Those attempts later led scholars of Arab philosophy to describe it incorrectly as a philosophy of “reconciliation.”
The dialectic of the relationship between kalām and philosophy naturally had to contain a contradiction.
That contradiction arose from the conservative reaction that later gave rise to Ashʿarite kalām.
As we have said, the Muʿtazilite stage of kalām prepared the way for the birth of Arab philosophy.
When this stage was nearing its end, kalām was close to giving up its place in the development of Arab thought and leaving that role to philosophy.
But then the conservative reaction appeared and tried to take philosophy’s place.
The conditions for the birth of philosophy had already matured, and philosophy therefore had to emerge.
As a result, the place once occupied by Muʿtazilite kalām was taken by two opposing forces.
On one side stood conservative Ashʿarite kalām, which tried to interrupt the development of Arab thought and return it to the method of the People of the Sunna.
On the other stood philosophy, which represented the natural qualitative transformation produced by the accumulated process of development.

The most visible expression of this contradiction was the repeated campaigns of intellectual, and sometimes physical, repression directed against philosophy and philosophers—and even against the natural and mathematical sciences.

Al-Ghazālī played the most important and influential role in this process of repression. His influence became so great that medieval theological philosophy in Europe later used his ideas as weapons against its own opponents.
How and when did Arab-Islamic thought first come into real contact with Aristotle’s logic, or with Greek logic more generally?
Establishing the historical setting of this question is not an end in itself.

Our aim is to discover, in light of the particular historical conditions, how and when Arab-Islamic thought came to need Aristotle’s logic in order to advance according to its own internal development, in connection with the development of Arab-Islamic society itself, especially during the seventh and eighth centuries.
Historians of Arab-Islamic thought are almost unanimous that logic was the first part of the Greek philosophical heritage to become known to Arab-Islamic thinkers.
But when did this happen, and how?

There are several historical signs from which we can conclude that the process began during the first century AH, or the seventh century CE—that is, during the Umayyad period, from 40 to 132 AH/661 to 750 CE.
Among these signs are the following:

1 — It is historically well established that, during the Umayyad period, representatives of the different trends within Arab-Islamic thought entered into extensive debates with representatives of non-Islamic religious schools that already existed in several centres in Syria and Mesopotamia at the time of the Arab conquests, as well as with Persian religious movements.

These exchanges covered many questions of thought and religious doctrine, together with philosophical questions connected to them and to the ideological conflicts taking shape in the new society under Umayyad rule.
The religious schools we have mentioned were strongly influenced by Greek philosophy and especially by Aristotelian logic.
Some researchers even state specifically that these schools taught Aristotle’s logic as far as the end of chapter seven of the Prior Analytics.

Can we really imagine, then, that contact between Arab-Islamic thinkers and these schools could have become so extensive during the Umayyad period without including logic—or at least some questions of logic?

This is especially difficult to believe when we know that the debates conducted by representatives of these schools with Arab-Islamic thinkers were often based on Greek philosophy and on the method of Aristotelian logic.
2 — Historians of Arab-Islamic thought such as al-Shahrastānī tell us that the earliest theologians, including Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, who died in 131 AH/748 CE, “read the books of the philosophers.”

Other historians tell us that the “sciences of the ancients” entered Muslim lands during the first century AH, when the Muslims conquered non-Arab peoples, although these sciences did not become widespread because the early religious authorities discouraged people from engaging with them.

Among these historians, the expression “sciences of the ancients” referred specifically to the sciences of Greek philosophy. Logic was either included among them or treated as their introduction and foundation.

So here too we must ask: how can we imagine that theologians of the first century AH were reading the books of philosophers, as al-Shahrastānī says, and that the sciences of the ancients were entering Muslim lands during that same century, as Ibn Kathīr says, while those theologians somehow remained untouched by logic?
After all, as we have already seen, historians of Arab-Islamic thought agree that logic was the first part of the Greek philosophical heritage to become known to Arab-Islamic thinkers.

If we accept what these historical signs suggest and say that Arab-Islamic thought began to encounter logic during the first century AH, in the Umayyad period, we immediately face another historical claim widely accepted by historians.
According to this claim, logic was not translated into Arabic until the Abbasid period.

Historians disagree only about when this translation began: during the reign of the second Abbasid caliph, Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, from 754 to 775 CE, or during the reign of the seventh Abbasid caliph, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn, from 813 to 833 CE.

This view would move the beginning of Arab knowledge of Aristotelian logic to around the middle of the second century AH, or the middle of the eighth century CE, or even to the period between the second and third centuries AH, in the ninth century CE.

The Andalusian judge Ṣāʿid, who died in 462 AH/1070 CE, reports that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who died in 142 AH/760 CE, translated three of Aristotle’s works on logic from Pahlavi into Arabic while serving as a secretary under al-Manṣūr.
These were the Categories (Kategorias), On Interpretation (Pari Hermenias), and the Analytics (Analytica). He also translated Porphyry of Tyre’s Isagoge, or Introduction to the Categories.
Al-Qifṭī and Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa repeat the same report from Ṣāʿid.
We have not found the substance of this report in the works of Muslim historians who wrote before Ṣāʿid.
The Orientalist Paul Kraus, however, rejects the claim that these translations were made by ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ.

He attributes them instead to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who lived under the Abbasid caliphs al-Mahdī and al-Hādī after al-Manṣūr. Kraus bases this conclusion on manuscript no. 338 in the Saint Joseph Library in Beirut.
He also argues that these works were not translations of Aristotle’s books themselves, but summaries of commentaries on them.
